steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the Impact section of an encyclopedia article on the 2021 Microsoft Exchange Server data breach: who was hit, why smaller organizations suffered most, which countries and sectors were targeted, notable victims, and the ransomware that followed.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Scale of the attack and types of targets
- Why small organizations were hit hardest
- Most attacked countries and sectors
- Discovery and notable victims
- Other threat groups exploiting the flaws
- Ransomware: DearCry and the Acer attack

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Scale
  - vulnerabilities used to spy on wide range of targets; est. 250,000 servers
  - Tom Burt (Microsoft VP, Customer Security & Trust): disease researchers, law offices, universities, defense contractors, NGOs, think tanks
- Small organizations
  - automatic updates usually disabled by admins to avoid downtime / software problems
  - updates installed manually after testing with existing software and server-setup
  - smaller orgs: small budget, in-house or local IT providers without cybersecurity expertise -> not done until necessary, if ever
  - small and medium businesses, schools, local governments primary victims, more likely unpatched
  - rural victims "largely on their own", no IT service providers
  - 11 March 2021, Check Point Research: in prior 24 hours "the number of exploitation attempts on organizations it tracks tripled every two to three hours."
- Countries / sectors (Check Point Research)
  - US 17%, Germany 6%, UK and Netherlands 5%, Russia 4%
  - government/military 23%, manufacturing 15%, banking and financial services 14%, software vendors 7%, healthcare 6%
- Discovery / victims
  - discovered when attackers seen downloading all emails of specific users on separate corporate Exchange servers
  - undisclosed Washington think tank: convincing social-engineering emails to contacts with a link
  - 11 March 2021: Norway's parliament, the Storting, victim; "data has been extracted."
  - European Banking Authority targeted; press release: impact "limited", "the confidentiality of the EBA systems and data has not been compromised"
- Other groups
  - ESET: "at least 10" APT groups; IT, cybersecurity, energy, software development, public utility, real estate, telecommunications, engineering; Middle Eastern and South American government agencies
  - one APT group: PowerShell downloaders, cryptocurrency mining
  - Cybereason CEO Lior Div on Hafnium: [quote: small and medium-sized enterprises; 1,000 times more devastating than SolarWinds]
- Ransomware
  - 12 March 2021: Microsoft Security Intelligence, "a new family of ransomware", DearCry, on initially infected servers; encrypts, servers unusable, demands payment
  - Microsoft: "There is no guarantee that paying the ransom will give you access to your files."
  - 18 March 2021: REvil affiliate claims stolen unencrypted data from Acer (Taiwanese hardware/electronics), undisclosed number of devices encrypted
  - Advanced Intel links it to Exchange exploits; Acer Exchange server first targeted 5 March 2021
  - $50 million ransom: "provide a decryptor, a vulnerability report, and the deletion of stolen files"; doubles to $100 million if not paid on 28 March 2021

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Hackers have used the vulnerabilities to spy on a wide range of targets, and an estimated 250,000 servers were affected. Tom Burt, who is Microsoft's vice president for Customer Security & Trust, wrote that the targets included disease researchers, law offices, universities, defense contractors, non-governmental organizations, and think tanks.

Server administrators typically disable automatic updates so they can avoid disruption from downtime and problems in software, and by convention the administrators install the updates manually after testing them with the existing software and server-setup; smaller organizations often have a smaller budget to do this in-house, or they outsource it to local IT providers that do not have expertise in cybersecurity, so it is often not done until it becomes a necessity, if it is ever done. Because of this, small and medium businesses and local institutions such as schools and local governments are known to be the primary victims of the attack, as they are more likely not to have received the updates that patch the exploit. Rural victims are noted to be "largely on their own", because they typically do not have access to IT service providers. On 11 March 2021, Check Point Research revealed that in the prior 24 hours "the number of exploitation attempts on organizations it tracks tripled every two to three hours."

Check Point Research has observed that the United States is the most attacked country, with 17% of all exploit attempts, and then Germany with 6%, the United Kingdom and the Netherlands both at 5%, and Russia with 4% of all exploits. The most targeted sector is government/military with 23% of exploit attempts, then manufacturing at 15%, banking and financial services at 14%, software vendors with 7% and healthcare at 6%.

- Discovery / victims
  - found when attackers downloaded all emails of specific users on separate corporate Exchange servers
  - unnamed Washington think tank: convincing social-engineering emails to contacts, click on link
  - 11 March 2021: the Storting (Norway) victim, "data has been extracted."
  - European Banking Authority targeted; press release: "limited", "the confidentiality of the EBA systems and data has not been compromised"
- Other groups
  - ESET: "at least 10" APT groups; IT, cybersecurity, energy, software development, public utility, real estate, telecommunications, engineering; Middle Eastern and South American agencies
  - one group: PowerShell downloaders, cryptocurrency mining
  - Lior Div (Cybereason) on Hafnium: "targeted small and medium-sized enterprises ... The assault against Microsoft Exchange is 1,000 times more devastating than the SolarWinds attack."
- Ransomware
  - 12 March 2021: "a new family of ransomware", DearCry; encrypts, servers unusable, payment demanded; Microsoft: "There is no guarantee that paying the ransom will give you access to your files."
  - 18 March 2021: REvil affiliate and Acer; Advanced Intel links to Exchange, Acer server targeted 5 March 2021
  - $50 million ransom ("provide a decryptor, a vulnerability report, and the deletion of stolen files"), $100 million if unpaid on 28 March 2021

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Hackers have used the vulnerabilities to spy on a wide range of targets, and an estimated 250,000 servers were affected. Tom Burt, who is Microsoft's vice president for Customer Security & Trust, wrote that the targets included disease researchers, law offices, universities, defense contractors, non-governmental organizations, and think tanks.

Server administrators typically disable automatic updates so they can avoid disruption from downtime and problems in software, and by convention the administrators install the updates manually after testing them with the existing software and server-setup; smaller organizations often have a smaller budget to do this in-house, or they outsource it to local IT providers that do not have expertise in cybersecurity, so it is often not done until it becomes a necessity, if it is ever done. Because of this, small and medium businesses and local institutions such as schools and local governments are known to be the primary victims of the attack, as they are more likely not to have received the updates that patch the exploit. Rural victims are noted to be "largely on their own", because they typically do not have access to IT service providers. On 11 March 2021, Check Point Research revealed that in the prior 24 hours "the number of exploitation attempts on organizations it tracks tripled every two to three hours."

Check Point Research has observed that the United States is the most attacked country, with 17% of all exploit attempts, and then Germany with 6%, the United Kingdom and the Netherlands both at 5%, and Russia with 4% of all exploits. The most targeted sector is government/military with 23% of exploit attempts, then manufacturing at 15%, banking and financial services at 14%, software vendors with 7% and healthcare at 6%.

The attack was discovered when attackers were found downloading all of the emails belonging to specific users on separate corporate Exchange servers. A Washington think tank, which was not named, reported that attackers sent convincing emails to its contacts in a social engineering attack that encouraged the recipients to click on a link. On 11 March 2021, Norway's parliament, the Storting, reported that it was a victim of the hack, and stated that "data has been extracted."

The European Banking Authority also reported being targeted in the attack, and later it stated in a press release that the scope of the impact on its systems was "limited" and that "the confidentiality of the EBA systems and data has not been compromised".

The security company ESET identified "at least 10" advanced persistent threat groups that were compromising IT, cybersecurity, energy, software development, public utility, real estate, telecommunications and engineering businesses, and also Middle Eastern and South American governmental agencies. One APT group was found deploying PowerShell downloaders and using the affected servers for cryptocurrency mining. Lior Div, the CEO of Cybereason, noted that the APT group Hafnium "targeted small and medium-sized enterprises ... The assault against Microsoft Exchange is 1,000 times more devastating than the SolarWinds attack."

On 12 March 2021, Microsoft Security Intelligence announced "a new family of ransomware" called DearCry, which was being deployed to the servers that had initially been infected. It encrypts the device contents, makes the servers unusable and demands payment to recover the files. Microsoft stated: "There is no guarantee that paying the ransom will give you access to your files."

On 18 March 2021, an affiliate of the ransomware cybergang REvil claimed that they had stolen unencrypted data from Acer, the Taiwanese hardware and electronics corporation, and that an undisclosed number of devices had been encrypted. The cybersecurity firm Advanced Intel linked this data breach and ransomware attack to the Microsoft Exchange exploits. Advanced Intel detected that one of Acer's Microsoft Exchange servers was first targeted on 5 March 2021. REvil has demanded a ransom of $50 million U.S. dollars, and claimed that if this is paid they would "provide a decryptor, a vulnerability report, and the deletion of stolen files", and also stated that the ransom would double to $100 million U.S. dollars if it was not paid on 28 March 2021.
